videos.title: OpenAI hacked, Jev, Google’s RSI, Qwen 3.8 Omni, Bonsai 2, new Gemini Live: AI NEWS
videos.ai_tech_id: Multi-model AI news roundup: Jev (Typesafe AI "System One" models), Google Dream RSI (recursive self-improvement), Qwen 3.8 Omni Flash & Live Translate (Alibaba), Gemini 3.8 Live w/ extended thinking (Google), Bonsai 2 27B, OpenAI Astra for Law, OpenAI security breach
summary: AI Search's daily news roundup covers roughly twenty separate AI releases and stories from the past day, anchored by a reported OpenAI hack, the debut of a fast/cheap decision-model called Jev from Typesafe AI, and Google's "Dream RSI" recursive self-improvement demo alongside a new extended-thinking version of Gemini Live (3.8).

Other segments cover Qwen's 3.8 Omni Flash and Live Translate models from Alibaba, the open-weight Bonsai 2 27B model, OpenAI's Astra for Law product, and a string of smaller items including Meridian, R2T2, Jing Dao's world-simulation research, Xiaomi's real-time RL work, and a project claiming to have decrypted a WWII-era German Enigma message with modern compute.

As a news-digest video, its value is breadth rather than depth: it functions as a single checkpoint across labs (Google, Alibaba/Qwen, OpenAI, and several smaller AI startups) for anyone tracking model releases, security incidents, and infrastructure announcements from the last 24 hours.

videos.title: GPT Image 2.5 vs. Gemini 2: which model nails a camouflaged spider in one shot?
videos.ai_tech_id: GPT Image 2.5 (OpenAI) vs. Gemini 2 (Google) image generation
summary: Futurepedia runs a head-to-head image-generation test between OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 and Google's Gemini 2, using a single shared prompt: generate a highly detailed image of a spider camouflaged in its environment.

GPT Image 2.5 successfully blends the spider into the surrounding texture while holding up under close detail, whereas Gemini 2's output is described as not close to matching that level of camouflage or texture fidelity.

The short clip frames this single-prompt test as further evidence that GPT Image 2.5 currently leads on complex, texture-heavy scene generation compared to Gemini 2, a useful data point for anyone choosing an image model for detailed compositional work.

videos.title: I Tested Jev on 12 Real Use Cases. My Honest Thoughts.
summary: Nate Herk tests Jev, an AI model built to make fast, low-cost decisions rather than write text or hold conversations, across twelve real-world use cases to see where it actually fits in production automations.

He benchmarks its speed and cost against traditional language models on tasks like email classification, then shows live builds including an X feed classifier Chrome extension and a real-time paper-trading prototype, walking through comments, community automations, and meeting/video-clip handling along the way.

The video's conclusion is a practical evaluation framework rather than a pure endorsement: Jev is positioned as strong for narrow, high-volume decision tasks where speed and cost matter most, with Nate flagging specific scenarios where it underperforms slower, more capable models.

videos.title: How to Build Codex Skills Better than 99% of People
videos.ai_tech_id: OpenAI Codex "skills" (custom agent recipes) tested across multiple models
summary: Nate Herk breaks down a six-step framework for building reusable "skills" inside OpenAI Codex, treating a skill as a recipe that lets an agent repeat a process consistently: reverse-engineer a strong output, give each skill one job and one trigger, choose the right autonomy/freedom level, build in verification loops, test cheaper models first, and iterate after every run.

He then applies the framework live, running his own "X Article" skill across several models he refers to as Sol, Terra, and Luna, and comparing those results against a model called Astra to see which produces the most usable output for the least cost.

The video positions disciplined skill design, not just prompting, as the real lever for getting consistent agent output inside Codex, and demonstrates a repeatable process for choosing which underlying model to route a given skill to.

videos.title: Most People Are Still New To AI
videos.ai_tech_id: General AI adoption commentary (references Grok Bot, Hermes agents as examples of "insider" AI chatter)
summary: Sabrina Ramonov argues that AI hype is concentrated in a handful of "bubble" cities (San Francisco, LA, New York) where debates rage over the newest agents, model versions, and benchmarks, while most people outside those circles are still asking basic questions.

She lists the actual questions she hears most often from her audience, such as which AI app to install, how to set it up on mobile, how to talk to it, and how to write a better prompt, contrasting that with insider chatter about things like Grok Bot or Hermes agents that means nothing to a typical user.

The takeaway is aimed at anyone selling AI consulting, coaching, or education: meet customers where they actually are, with patient, first-step explanations, rather than assuming they're tracking the same cutting-edge releases as the AI-Twitter crowd.

videos.title: Stop Feeling Behind On AI News
videos.ai_tech_id: General AI tooling commentary (ChatGPT vs. Gemini positioning)
summary: Sabrina Ramonov pushes back on AI-news FOMO, explaining that she deliberately does not try to track every new tool, model update, or viral launch in real time.

Her stated approach is to wait a few months while early adopters stress-test new releases, surface bugs and security issues, and figure out which use cases actually matter, arguing she's still effectively "early" relative to most users even on a multi-month delay.

She closes with a practical prescription, pick fewer tools, learn them more deeply, and spend less time on social media, noting that the most common question she still gets from her audience is simply whether to use ChatGPT or Gemini.

videos.title: The ONLY 10 Ways to Make Money with AI in 2026 (Ranked List)
videos.ai_tech_id: General AI monetization roundup; references her own Blotato.com AI social-content automation SaaS
summary: Sabrina Ramonov presents a ranked list of ten ways to make money with AI in 2026, with the stated ranking criteria being how easy each path is for a complete beginner to start earning from.

She frames the list around her own background, from founding an NLP-in-healthcare startup, through a pivot into real-time AI call guidance for sales and support that was later acquired by Pegasystems, to her current work teaching AI to a mass audience and running Blotato, her AI-driven social content distribution SaaS.

The video functions as both a monetization guide and a personal case study, using her own trajectory, healthcare AI, then AI-powered customer support, then AI content/education, as proof points for how the ranked opportunities can play out in practice.
